text: "What do I need to open in the firewall for this?" is genuinely the single most common blocker to standing up a self-hosted IR in a real enterprise. The honest answer is reassuring: outbound only, on port 443. No inbound rule, no new hole punched in the firewall for the outside world to reach in.

Every connection is initiated by the self-hosted IR machine itself, reaching out to four real destinations, all over standard HTTPS on port 443: Azure Data Factory, Azure Relay carrying the control-channel traffic, the Microsoft Download Center for updates, and Azure Key Vault when you're using it for credentials. A small, well-known, documented set — not "the whole internet."

Plenty of real networks don't allow direct outbound internet access at all — everything has to go through an internal proxy first. The Configuration Manager has a dedicated screen for exactly this: direct access with no proxy, the Windows system proxy, or a custom proxy with its own address, port, and credentials. Once set, all of the IR's outbound traffic routes through it.

Walking into a real security review with this picture covers nearly every question that comes up: no inbound exposure, a small and stable destination list, standard HTTPS rather than some custom port, and credentials that never touch the wire in the clear — Key Vault integration, which Lesson 48 covers, keeps secrets out of pipeline definitions entirely.

That closes out integration runtimes — Azure, self-hosted, and now the exact security story behind connecting them safely to on-premises data. Next, Chapter 8: Monitoring and Error Handling, watching pipelines run in production and building ones that actually recover when something breaks.
